title: Lowa Hiking Boots for Kenyan Hikers: Which Model, Which Size, Which Trail

excerpt: Which Lowa hiking boots suit Kenya? We match the Renegade, Camino and Tibet to Kenyan trails, explain Lowa sizing, and show what to check on a thrifted pair in Nairobi.

content:
Lowa hiking boots suit Kenyan hikers who want one sturdy, waterproof pair for muddy forest days, volcanic ash and the long walk up Mt Kenya. The Renegade GTX Mid covers most day hikes near Nairobi, the Camino Evo GTX carries heavier loads on multi-day treks, and the Tibet Evo GTX handles rough, rocky ground.

The hard part is choosing between them, getting the size right and judging a second-hand pair, because most Lowa hiking boots reach Kenya through thrifted stock rather than brand-new shelves. Below we match each Lowa line to real Kenyan trails, explain how the boots fit, and show what to check on a used pair before you hand over your money.

Quick Facts

  • Brand origin: Lowa was founded in 1923 by Lorenz Wagner, a cobbler in Jetzendorf, Bavaria, Germany.
  • Best-known model: the Renegade GTX Mid, first produced in 1997 and still one of the best-selling outdoor boots in the world.
  • Weight range: about 590 g per boot (Renegade Evo GTX Mid) to roughly 880 g per boot (Tibet Evo GTX, 1,760 g a pair).
  • Waterproofing: GTX models use a Gore-Tex lining; LL models use a leather lining for dry, warm conditions.
  • Where made: Lowa builds its boots in Europe, with factories in Germany, Italy and Slovakia.
  • Kenyan sweet spot: Renegade for Ngong Hills, Longonot and Elephant Hill; Camino or Tibet for Mt Kenya and Kilimanjaro.

What Are Lowa Hiking Boots Known For?

Lowa hiking boots are known for German-designed, European-made leather boots that feel comfortable out of the box yet last for years. The brand's reputation rests on supportive midsoles, Gore-Tex linings, Vibram rubber and boots that a factory can resole.

Lowa began in 1923 when Lorenz Wagner started making heavy work shoes for his neighbours in Jetzendorf, a small village north of Munich. The company opened its first factory in 1930, went bankrupt in 1953 and was rescued two years later by Wagner's daughter Berti and her husband Sepp Lederer. Today Lowa says it produces close to three million pairs a year and leads the outdoor footwear market in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. You can read the full timeline on the official Lowa history page.

Three pieces of technology turn up again and again on Lowa hiking boots, and they are worth knowing before you read a label:

  • Monowrap frame: a polyurethane frame that wraps the side of the boot, supporting the arch and holding the heel steady on uneven ground.
  • DuraPU and DynaPU midsoles: polyurethane layers, often injected as a softer cushioning layer over a firmer support layer, which keep their shape longer than the soft foams in trainers.
  • Heinen Terracare nubuck: a leather from a German tannery, used on the Renegade Evo and Camino Evo uppers.

For Kenyan hikers, that combination is why Lowa hiking boots make sense: our trails punish soft shoes. Red murram turns to grease on the Ngong Hills ridge in November, loose ash rolls under your feet on the Longonot crater rim, and the Aberdares bamboo zone can swallow a boot to the ankle. A firm frame and a deep Vibram tread cope with all three.

Which Lowa Hiking Boots Suit Kenyan Trails?

For most Kenyan hikers the Renegade GTX Mid is the right Lowa, because it handles day hikes and light trekking. Choose the Camino Evo GTX for multi-day loads and the Tibet Evo GTX for rocky, high and rough terrain.

Renegade GTX Mid: the all-rounder

Of all Lowa hiking boots, the Renegade is the one most Nairobi hikers should look at first. It is light for a leather boot, flexes enough for a long day and keeps water out through the short rains. The current Renegade Evo GTX Mid uses Heinen Terracare nubuck, a double-injection DuraPU and DynaPU midsole, the Monowrap frame and a Vibram Rene Trac outsole, with two-zone lacing so you can set the forefoot and ankle separately.

In practice that suits hikes such as a muddy Table Mountain day in the Aberdares, the steep red-soil climb at Ol Donyo Sabuk or the 13.5 km rim of Mt Longonot; the first two are on our guided hike list. We stock the Lowa Renegade Evo GTX Mid when pairs come in, and our older Renegade Evo GTX Mid write-up goes deeper into that one model.

Renegade LL Mid: the dry-season option

LL stands for leather lining. Lowa recommends the Renegade LL for on-trail day hikes and light backpacking in dry climates, and it is made in Slovakia. Without a membrane the boot breathes better, which helps on hot, dusty walks such as Hell's Gate in February, but it will soak through in a proper downpour. Treat it as a second pair, not your only pair.

Camino Evo GTX: for loaded packs

Among Lowa hiking boots, the Camino is a step up in support. Lowa lists it as a medium-weight backpacking and rugged hiking boot at 775 g a boot, with a DuraPU midsole, Vibram Apptrail II outsole, roller eyelets, a flat climbing zone at the toe and a sole that Lowa can resole at its German factory. If you plan four or five days on Mt Kenya's Sirimon or Chogoria routes with a 12-15 kg pack, the Camino's stiffer platform is kinder to tired feet than a Renegade.

Tibet Evo GTX: for rock and altitude

The Tibet is the heaviest of the common Lowa hiking boots at about 1,760 g a pair. It uses a Vibram Apptrail Divo sole with a self-cleaning tread, and it is stiffer and more protective on sharp rock. That stiffness is overkill for Karura Forest, but on the loose scree below Point Lenana (4,985 m) or the long descent from Kilimanjaro's crater, a rigid boot stops your toes jamming and your ankles rolling.

Lighter Lowa shoes: Innox and Ferrox

Lowa also makes lighter, trainer-like hiking shoes such as the Innox Pro GTX and Ferrox GTX. They suit fast summer walking and short day hikes on firm trails like the Ngong Hills in the dry months. On muddy Aberdares days, most hikers will be happier in a mid-height boot.

How Do Lowa Hiking Boots Fit?

Lowa hiking boots fit fairly true to size, with a medium-volume forefoot and a snug, well-held heel. Lowa's own advice is to start with your normal street-shoe size and try boots on in the afternoon, wearing the socks you hike in.

Some retailers suggest going up half a size in Lowa hiking boots, especially if you wear thick socks or walk long, steep descents. A good test is simple: with the boot unlaced, slide your foot forward until your toes touch the front, then check that one finger fits behind your heel. Laced up, your heel should barely lift when you walk up a slope, and your toes should not touch the end when you step down hard.

Do Lowa hiking boots come in wide fits?

Yes, some Lowa hiking boots come in wide versions, most often the Renegade. Lowa labels men's widths as narrow (C), medium (D) and wide (E/EE), and women's as narrow (B), medium (C) and wide (D). If a Keen feels roomy and a Scarpa feels tight, a standard Lowa usually sits between them.

UK, EU and US sizes on Lowa labels

Thrifted Lowa hiking boots come from Europe and North America, so the tongue label may show UK, EU or US sizes, or all three. Go by the UK or EU figure you know from your other shoes, and always try the pair on rather than trusting the number alone. A UK 9 Lowa and a UK 9 trainer rarely feel the same.

Men's and women's Lowa models

Lowa women's boots, marked Ws on the label, are usually built on a women's last with a slimmer heel and lower volume, not just a smaller size. A woman with broad feet can often wear a men's Renegade comfortably, and a man with slim feet may find a Ws model fits better. Fit is what counts, not the label.

What Should You Check on Second-Hand Lowa Hiking Boots?

On second-hand Lowa hiking boots, check the midsole for cracks or crumbling, the tread depth, the stitching around the toe and the inside lining. A good used pair has plenty of life left; a poor one fails within weeks.

Quality thrifted gear is how most Kenyan hikers can afford a European boot, and Lowa hiking boots are good candidates because they are built to last and can be resoled. Still, every used pair has its own history, so look closely before you buy.

A six-point check for a thrifted pair

  1. Midsole: press your thumb hard into the side of the midsole. It should feel firm and spring back. Polyurethane midsoles can break down with age, even on boots that were barely worn, so fine cracks, powdery crumbling or a sole peeling away from the upper are reasons to walk away.
  2. Tread: the Vibram lugs should still have sharp edges, especially under the heel and the ball of the foot. Rounded, flat lugs will not grip wet murram or bamboo mud.
  3. Toe rand and stitching: look where the rubber toe cap meets the leather. Small scuffs are normal; lifting rubber or broken stitches let water in.
  4. Lining: run your hand inside the heel. A Gore-Tex lining should be smooth and intact; holes or worn patches mean the boot will no longer stay dry.
  5. Heel counter: squeeze the back of the boot. It should feel stiff. A collapsed heel cup will not hold your foot on descents.
  6. Insole and footbed: lift the insole out. Worn insoles are cheap to replace, but deep foot-shaped grooves tell you how much walking the boot has done.

How to tell genuine Lowa hiking boots from fakes

Counterfeit outdoor boots exist in every market, so it pays to know a few general signs of a genuine Lowa. Look for a sewn-in tongue label showing the model name, size and a production code, a clear yellow Vibram logo moulded into the sole on models that use Vibram, and a Gore-Tex tag or logo on GTX models. Stitching should be tight and even, and the leather should feel thick rather than plasticky. None of these signs is proof on its own, so judge the whole boot, and if something feels off, ask questions or look at another pair.

Lowa, Keen or Quechua: Which Boot Fits Your Hiking?

Pick Lowa hiking boots if you want a firm, supportive leather boot for mixed terrain and altitude. Choose Keen for wide feet and toe room, or Quechua for a light, budget boot for occasional day hikes near Nairobi.

Each brand has its place. The Keen Targhee Mid Waterproof has a broad toe box and a rubber toe bumper that many Kenyan hikers with wide feet love. The Quechua waterproof hiking boot is lighter on the feet and on the wallet, which suits beginners doing Karura or Oloolua. Lowa hiking boots sit above both for support and long-term durability, which is why they are worth considering if you hike every month or are training for Mt Kenya. How Do You Care for Lowa Hiking Boots in Kenya's Mud and Dust?

Care for Lowa hiking boots by brushing off mud after every hike, drying them slowly away from direct heat, and re-treating the nubuck with a water repellent every few months. Kenyan red soil and volcanic dust wear leather faster than you might expect.

After a muddy hike

Knock the worst of the mud off your Lowa hiking boots at the trailhead, then rinse the boots with clean water at home and brush the welt and tread with a soft brush. Take the insoles out and stuff the boots loosely with newspaper. Let them dry in shade at room temperature; never leave them in the sun on a car dashboard, beside a jiko or on top of a water heater, because heat dries out the leather and can weaken the glue between sole and upper.

After a dusty hike

Fine dust from Longonot, Hell's Gate or Suswa works into nubuck and acts like sandpaper on the stitching. Brush it out while it is dry, then wipe the boots with a damp cloth. Dust clogging the Gore-Tex lining from outside also reduces breathability, so clean boots stay drier inside too.

Re-waterproofing and storage

When water stops beading on the leather and starts darkening it, apply a nubuck-friendly waterproofing spray or wax to clean, slightly damp boots. Before the long rains in March and the short rains in October, this is worth doing as a routine. Between hikes, store Lowa hiking boots in a dry, airy place rather than a sealed bag; Nairobi's damp months can grow mould inside a closed cupboard.

When to resole

Many Lowa hiking boots, including the Camino Evo GTX, are designed to be resoled. Once the tread lugs are worn flat but the uppers, lining and midsole are still sound, a resole can give the boot a second life. Ask a skilled cobbler what is possible with your model before the sole wears right through to the midsole.

Pro Tips for Lowa Owners

  • Lace in two zones: keep the forefoot comfortable and tighten the upper hooks before a long descent such as Longonot's crater path.
  • Wear proper socks: merino wool hiking socks cushion the foot and manage sweat on 6-8 hour days.
  • Add gaiters in mud: waterproof leg gaiters keep Aberdares bog water from pouring over the collar.
  • Break them in on short walks: walk 20-30 km around Karura or Ngong Road Forest before any big climb.
  • Carry spare laces: a snapped lace on Mt Kenya is a long, awkward problem; a spare pair weighs almost nothing.

Are Lowa Hiking Boots Worth It for Mt Kenya and Kilimanjaro?

Lowa hiking boots are worth it for Mt Kenya and Kilimanjaro if you choose a supportive model such as the Camino Evo GTX or Tibet Evo GTX, size it for thick socks and break it in well before the climb.

For Lowa hiking boots on a big mountain, the cold is the main test. Summit nights on both mountains start around midnight and can drop well below freezing, so a waterproof, insulating leather boot matters. A Renegade will get many fit hikers up Mt Kenya's Sirimon or Naro Moru routes to Point Lenana, especially in the drier January-February and August-September windows, but the extra stiffness of a Camino or Tibet pays off on scree and long, loaded descents. Pair your boots with warm layers and a good headlamp from our Mt Kenya packing list.

A sample Lowa choice by trip

  • Day hike near Nairobi (Ngong Hills, Ol Donyo Sabuk): Renegade GTX Mid or Renegade LL Mid in the dry season.
  • Long, muddy day (Elephant Hill, Table Mountain): Renegade GTX Mid with gaiters.
  • Four to five days on Mt Kenya: Camino Evo GTX, or a Renegade if you travel light.
  • Six to eight days on Kilimanjaro: Camino Evo GTX or Tibet Evo GTX.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Lowa boots good for hiking in Kenya?

Lowa boots are a strong choice for hiking in Kenya because their Gore-Tex linings, Vibram soles and firm Monowrap frames handle red-soil mud, volcanic ash and rocky ground. The Renegade GTX Mid suits most day hikes near Nairobi, while the Camino and Tibet models suit Mt Kenya and Kilimanjaro. Fit matters more than the brand, so try a pair before you buy.

Where are Lowa boots made?

Lowa boots are made in Europe. The company is based in Jetzendorf, Germany, and builds boots in Germany, Italy and Slovakia; it bought the Italian maker Riko Sport in 2019. The country is printed on the tongue label or inside the boot. A European-made boot with a clear label, model name and size is a good sign when you buy second-hand.

Do Lowa hiking boots run big or small?

Lowa hiking boots generally run true to size, so start with your usual street-shoe size. Many hikers go half a size up for thick socks and long descents. Try boots in the afternoon when your feet are slightly swollen, wearing your hiking socks, and check for one finger's width behind your heel before you lace up.

How long do Lowa hiking boots last?

Lowa hiking boots often last several years of regular hiking, and many models can be resoled once the tread wears down. Lifespan depends on how often you hike, the terrain and care. Cleaning off mud, drying boots away from heat and re-waterproofing the leather all add years. Check the polyurethane midsole on older pairs, as it can crack with age.

Is the Lowa Renegade waterproof?

The Lowa Renegade GTX Mid is waterproof because it has a Gore-Tex lining, which keeps water out while letting sweat escape. The Renegade LL Mid is different: it has a leather lining and is meant for dry, warm conditions. Check for "GTX" on the label, and remember that water can still come in over the collar in deep mud without gaiters.

Final Thoughts

Pick the Lowa by the mountain, not by the colour, and a good pair will carry you for years. Lowa hiking boots give Kenyan hikers German build quality, a supportive frame and a waterproof lining: the Renegade for day hikes around Nairobi, the Camino for loaded treks, the Tibet for scree and summit days.
